system: You are a research mathematician working alone, with no tools and no internet access. Answer only in the requested JSON format. Write mathematics in English, using LaTeX ($...$) for formulas.
prompt:
Solve the following problem as completely as you can.

<problem>
For $N\ge 1$ let $[N]=\{1,\dots,N\}$ and let $s(N)$ be the largest size of a set $A\subseteq[N]$ containing no triple $x,\;x+d^2,\;x+2d^2$ with $x,d\in\mathbb N$, $d\ge1$ (a non-trivial $3$-term arithmetic progression whose common difference is a perfect square). Let $r_3(N)$ be the largest size of a subset of $[N]$ with no non-trivial $3$-term progression; trivially $s(N)\ge r_3(N)\ge N\exp(-c\sqrt{\log N})$ (Behrend), while the best known upper bound is of the form $s(N)\ll N(\log\log N)^{-c}$.

(1) Does there exist an absolute constant $c>0$ such that $s(N)\ll N\exp\!\big(-(\log N)^{c}\big)$, i.e. does a Kelley–Meka-type bound hold when the common difference is restricted to squares?

(2) Is $\log\big(N/s(N)\big)\asymp\log\big(N/r_3(N)\big)$, or can sets avoiding square-difference progressions be substantially denser than $3$-AP-free sets, e.g. $s(N)\ge N\exp(-(\log N)^{1/2-c})$ for some $c>0$?
</problem>

<finite_instance>

</finite_instance>

<required_candidate_format>

</required_candidate_format>

Return
- text: your full solution or best partial progress: definitions, the argument, and a clear final answer. If you cannot solve it, state exactly what you proved and what remains.
- claimed_status: "solved" only if you believe the problem (or, when given, the finite instance) is fully solved; "partial" for real progress; "unsolved" otherwise.
- candidate: if a finite instance is given, the object you propose, exactly in the required JSON shape; otherwise null.

{"text":"Both parts are, to the best of my knowledge, open research problems; I record the known results, rigorous partial observations, and the obstacles.

KNOWN RESULTS. Upper bound: Prendiville (Discrete Analysis 2017, homogeneous polynomial Szemerédi) gives $s(N)\ll N(\log\log N)^{-c}$; nothing of the form $N/(\log N)^c$ is known for difference $d^2$. Shifted case: Peluse–Sah–Sawhney (2023) proved a Kelley–Meka bound $N\exp(-(\log N)^c)$ for progressions with common difference $y^2-1$; the shift makes $y\equiv 1\pmod q$ trivial solutions available for every $q$, removing local obstructions, and they state the unshifted case as open. Lower bound: only the trivial $s(N)\ge r_3(N)\ge N\exp(-c\sqrt{\log N})$.

RIGOROUS OBSERVATIONS.
(a) Since $s(N)\ge r_3(N)$, the assertion $\log(N/s(N))\asymp\log(N/r_3(N))$ would force $r_3(N)\le N\exp(-c\sqrt{\log N})$, i.e. Behrend-sharpness for Roth, far beyond the best known $r_3(N)\ll N\exp(-c(\log N)^{1/12})$. So the only accessible half of (2) is whether Behrend can be beaten.
(b) Lemma 1: if $q\ge 2$ is squarefree and $B\subseteq\mathbb Z_q$ has no $b,b+t,b+2t$ with $t\not\equiv 0$ a square mod $q$, then $s(qM)\ge |B|\,r_3(M)$. Proof: $A=\{b+qy: b\in B, y\in A_0\}$ with $A_0$ 3-AP-free; a progression $x,x+d^2,x+2d^2\subseteq A$ forces $d^2\equiv 0\pmod q$, so $q\mid d$, $d=qd'$, same residue $b$, and $y,y+qd'^2,y+2qd'^2\in A_0$, contradiction. Lemma 2: such $B$ has $|B|\le 2q/3$ (each element of the complement lies in at most $3|Q^*|$ of the $q|Q^*|$ square-difference progressions). Hence $\log\frac{N}{s(N)}\le \log\frac{q}{|B|}+\log\frac{N/q}{r_3(N/q)}$ with $\log(q/|B|)\ge \log(3/2)$: local-times-Behrend constructions change the exponent $c\sqrt{\log N}$ only by $O(\log q/\sqrt{\log N})$ for $q=N^{o(1)}$, and for $q=N^{\theta}$ they would require dense square-progression-free sets in $\mathbb Z_q$ (a harder cyclic version of the same problem). So this natural route cannot give $s(N)\ge N\exp(-(\log N)^{1/2-c})$.
(c) Obstacle to (1): for a prime $p$ and a 3-AP-free $B\subseteq\mathbb Z_p$ of density $\delta=\exp(-c\sqrt{\log p})$, the set $A=\{x\le N: x\bmod p\in B\}$ has density $\delta$ but only $\approx\delta N\sqrt N/p$ square-difference progressions (those with $p\mid d$) versus the expected $\delta^3N^{3/2}$, a deficit $1/(p\delta^2)$ with $p$ up to $\exp(C\log^2(1/\delta))$. Any density-increment proof must pass to progressions $a+p\mathbb Z$ (which renormalises to the same problem on $N/p$ points) uniformly for moduli of this size; this is exactly what the shift $y^2-1$ avoids and what has not been done for $y^2$. For $\delta=\exp(-(\log N)^c)$, $c<1/2$, this is not a priori fatal, so the conjecture remains plausible.
(d) Curiosity: the squares $\{n^2\le N\}$ are $s$-free, since $n_1^2,n_2^2,n_3^2$ in progression with difference $d^2$ would give $n_2^4-d^4=(n_1n_3)^2$, contradicting Fermat.

ANSWER. (1) Open; conjecturally yes, with best proven bound $N(\log\log N)^{-c}$. (2) Open; no construction beating Behrend is known and the natural local constructions provably give only constant-factor gains; the expected answer is $\log(N/s(N))\asymp\sqrt{\log N}\asymp\log(N/r_3(N))$, but even the upper half of this would imply Behrend-sharpness for Roth's theorem and is out of reach.","claimed_status":"unsolved","candidate":null}

KNOWN RESULTS. Upper bound: Prendiville (Discrete Analysis 2017, homogeneous polynomial Szemerédi) gives $s(N)\ll N(\log\log N)^{-c}$; nothing of the form $N/(\log N)^c$ is known for difference $d^2$. Lower bound: only the trivial $s(N)\ge r_3(N)\ge N\exp(-c\sqrt{\log N})$.

RIGOROUS OBSERVATIONS.
(a) Since $s(N)\ge r_3(N)$, the assertion $\log(N/s(N))\asymp\log(N/r_3(N))$ would force $r_3(N)\le N\exp(-c\sqrt{\log N})$, i.e. Behrend-sharpness for Roth, far beyond the best known $r_3(N)\ll N\exp(-c(\log N)^{1/12})$. So the only accessible half of (2) is whether Behrend can be beaten.

Lemma 2: such $B$ has $|B|\le 2q/3$ (each element of the complement lies in at most $3|Q^*|$ of the $q|Q^*|$ square-difference progressions). Hence $\log\frac{N}{s(N)}\le \log\frac{q}{|B|}+\log\frac{N/q}{r_3(N/q)}$ with $\log(q/|B|)\ge \log(3/2)$: local-times-Behrend constructions change the exponent $c\sqrt{\log N}$ only by $O(\log q/\sqrt{\log N})$ for $q=N^{o(1)}$, and for $q=N^{\theta}$ they would require dense square-progression-free sets in $\mathbb Z_q$ (a harder cyclic version of the same problem). So this natural route cannot give $s(N)\ge N\exp(-(\log N)^{1/2-c})$.
(c) Obstacle to (1): for a prime $p$ and a 3-AP-free $B\subseteq\mathbb Z_p$ of density $\delta=\exp(-c\sqrt{\log p})$, the set $A=\{x\le N: x\bmod p\in B\}$ has density $\delta$ but only $\approx\delta N\sqrt N/p$ square-difference progressions (those with $p\mid d$) versus the expected $\delta^3N^{3/2}$, a deficit $1/(p\delta^2)$ with $p$ up to $\exp(C\log^2(1/\delta))$. Any density-increment proof must pass to progressions $a+p\mathbb Z$ (which renormalises to the same problem on $N/p$ points) uniformly for moduli of this size; this is exactly what the shift $y^2-1$ avoids and what has not been done for $y^2$. For $\delta=\exp(-(\log N)^c)$, $c<1/2$, this is not a priori fatal, so the conjecture remains plausible.
(d) Curiosity: the squares $\{n^2\le N\}$ are $s$-free, since $n_1^2,n_2^2,n_3^2$ in progression with difference $d^2$ would give $n_2^4-d^4=(n_1n_3)^2$, contradicting Fermat.

ANSWER. (1) Open; conjecturally yes, with best proven bound $N(\log\log N)^{-c}$. (2) Open; no construction beating Behrend is known and the natural local constructions provably give only constant-factor gains; the expected answer is $\log(N/s(N))\asymp\sqrt{\log N}\asymp\log(N/r_3(N))$, but even the upper half of this would imply Behrend-sharpness for Roth's theorem and is out of reach.
